verdicts.note: Honest comparison for one developer. Compact: the own module wins. It removes better-auth and its 17 direct packages, @better-auth/expo and the client libraries, the catch-all bridge route and the Better Auth tables; it adds the official @fastify/cookie (2 dependencies, 18 npm maintainers) and roughly 300 to 500 lines plus tests, and gives staff and the student device keys one auth path. Sustainable: closer than the finding says. Better Auth is now Vercel-backed, MIT, with 4.7M+ weekly downloads and 850+ contributors, but it supports only the latest version and ships minors with schema changes (1.7.0 made Account.issuer required), so one developer pays a recurring upgrade and advisory-triage cost. An own module has no upstream churn, but every security bug is ours. Several plan rules need own code in both paths (per-address and per-account counters, 3-device cap, approval check, panel inactivity timeout, Origin check, client IP config). Net judgement: for this narrow scope the own module is the more compact option and about as sustainable, provided it follows a vetted reference (Lucia's auth_session.ts, the OWASP session cheat sheet) and behaviour tests cover atomic single use, attempt limits, constant-time comparison and token hashing. recommendation_issues.problem: Admin-only unlock after 50 consecutive failures hands outsiders a lockout lever. Instructor addresses are public; at the proposed 10 codes a day with 3 tries each, about 2 days of wrong guesses lock an account until an admin acts, for as many instructors as the attacker picks. NIST 3.2.2 names increasing waits (30 seconds up to an hour) as the alternative. Prefer growing waits with automatic unlock and a notice e-mail, with admin unlock only as an override. The loose IP limit the finding keeps also depends on a correctly derived client IP, which it does not cover (high miss on line 586).

The first option builds a second security-critical feature for one developer: a cross-device approval flow with code display, polling (push is not in the plan), binding, expiry, and a lost-phone recovery path that ASVS 6.4.4 wants at enrollment strength. The documented-deviation option is allowed by 6.3.3's own text and is the compact choice. Pair it with cheap controls: a 'new device signed in' e-mail, the short panel session from the medium miss on line 69, and the per-account limits from S04-02.

The sustainability evidence leaves out the Vercel acquisition (2026-07-07), and two of the listed custom-code items are configuration. The own module is still the more compact choice for this scope, but it should be presented as a trade-off with explicit conditions: HMAC-stored codes, atomic single use with an attempt count, crypto.timingSafeEqual, SHA-256-hashed session tokens, an Origin check for cookie requests, and a behaviour test for each, following Lucia's auth_session.ts and the OWASP session cheat sheet.

If Better Auth stays and the bearer plugin is added, requireSignature must be set to true. Its default is false, and Better Auth stores session tokens as plain values in the session table, so with the default any read of that table (pg_dump file, backup, replica, injection) yields tokens usable as 'Authorization: Bearer' for up to 30 days.

Retrying the mail job 'birkaç kez' only makes sense inside the code's 5-minute life. The job should expire with the code; otherwise a late retry delivers a dead code and the instructor burns attempts on it.

The 14-day inactivity example suits the instructor's own phone but not panel browsers on shared PCs (medium miss on line 69). ASVS 7.5.2 also asks for re-authentication with at least one factor before terminating sessions, which the recommendation omits.

The fixed review code is a second login path on the release server. ASVS 6.3.4 (L2) requires every pathway to be documented and held to the same controls: put it under the same per-account failure limit, keep it off by default and on only during review windows, and list it in the plan's security notes. Apple's built-in demo mode, with prior approval, is the alternative if no production bypass is wanted.

The closing rule 'Dil belirtmeyen toLowerCase ve toUpperCase kullanılmaz' must be limited to names. For e-mail addresses toLocaleLowerCase('tr') turns I into ı, and plain toLowerCase turns İ into i plus U+0307; addresses need their own ASCII rule (medium miss on line 69).

The named fallback, emailjs, is itself a single-maintainer package (5.0.3, one npm maintainer) with about 48.6 thousand weekly downloads against Nodemailer's 29.1 million, so it does not lower the risk. Since Nodemailer is MIT-0 with no dependencies and sits behind one mail interface, the realistic fallback is to keep the last good version pinned and fork if maintenance stops.

misses.finding: Better Auth 1.7.7 takes the client IP only from request headers (default x-forwarded-for); the documented Fastify bridge passes Fastify's headers and never the socket address, and the Fastify guide says nothing about IP configuration. In production, when no IP can be derived, every request falls into one shared per-path bucket: no forwarding header (no reverse proxy appears in the plan's Docker Compose list on line 714), or a multi-hop X-Forwarded-For with no trustedProxies configured (CDN plus proxy, or the load balancer of line 731 behind another hop). The built-in rules on that bucket are 3 per 60 s for /email-otp/send-verification-otp and /sign-in/email-otp, so instructor logins stall university-wide at term start and any outsider can keep the bucket full. Without a proxy that overwrites the header, a single client-supplied X-Forwarded-For is taken as-is, so the per-IP limit can be bypassed. None of this shows in the plan's tests: limiting is off in development and getIP returns 127.0.0.1 in test and development.
